narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: a patient, precise instructor who counts out loud, demonstrates from the front and the back, repeats every step slowly three times before speeding up, names mistakes kindly and never rushes
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In Bernalillo, New Mexico, Matachines dancers have performed for over three hundred years to enact the ancient battle between good and evil.
on_screen: Title card: Matachines · Mexico, United States, Peru · 17th century origin

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance emerged in Spain in the early 17th century, inspired by European traditions like the moresca, and was documented in 1642 by Juan de Esquivel Navarro.
It was imported into Latin America and the Southwestern United States by Spanish missionaries as an evangelizing tool known as the Dance of the Moors and Christians.
In Bernalillo, New Mexico, the Matachines de San Lorenzo have performed for over three hundred years.
on_screen: Map: Mexico, United States, Peru · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance serves a deeper religious purpose to venerate Mother Mary, local saints, Christ, or the Holy Trinity.
It functions as a celebration of native peoples in the Americas and their salvation through unity of faith and culture, portraying the triumph of good over evil.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves a chorus of dancers alongside specific characters performing formations that are all similar, though individual dance steps vary among different peoples and villages.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The tradition is accompanied by characteristic music associated with the danza de matachines, though specific instruments are not detailed in the sources beyond historical mentions of flutes in ancient variants.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear traditional ceremonial dress and masks that vary in style from village to village.
El Toro wears buffalo skins and the horns of a sacred ancestor.
All cultural artifacts associated with the dance are blessed by a priest.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Chief characters include El Monarca (Moctezuma or another tribal leader), the captains, La Malinche (the Native or Mestizo woman), El Toro (representing Satan), and the grandparents Abuelo and Abuela.
The dance is found from Peru up to northern New Mexico, and is written as matlachines and matlatzines in central Mexico.
Derived from European traditions such as the moresca and the bouffons documented in 16th and 17th-century Europe, adapted by Indigenous and Mestizo societies in the Americas.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Matachines (Mexico, United States, Peru). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
